tldr: Targeting the dangerous and delicate real-world task of EV battery disassembly, the authors built GOLEM, an open-source framework where full-body humanoid locomotion, navigation, manipulation, and memory can be independently swapped and benchmarked. Evaluating bolt extraction on a real Hyundai Ioniq 5 pack revealed exactly how error cascades across modules.
hero_caption: A Unitree H1-2 humanoid robot working on a real Hyundai Ioniq 5 battery pack alongside the RAPID gantry disassembly cell. It demonstrates how autonomous humanoids can seamlessly integrate into work environments designed for humans.
overview:
End-of-life electric vehicle (EV) lithium-ion batteries must be disassembled to recover valuable materials. However, this is hazardous work involving risks of high voltage, fires, and toxic gas emissions. Because pack designs vary widely, traditional dedicated industrial robots lack the flexibility to handle them all. Deploying life-sized humanoids into human-designed facilities offers a promising alternative. However, most existing end-to-end reinforcement learning policies are built for small robots, and a framework to fairly evaluate and integrate diverse algorithms on full-scale platforms capable of handling large batteries has been missing.

In this work, the authors introduce GOLEM, an open-source modular system architecture targeting the Unitree H1-2. By loosely coupling locomotion, upper-body manipulation, dynamic balance, navigation, and spatial memory behind abstract interfaces, GOLEM allows transparent switching between digital twins (MuJoCo and IsaacLab) and the physical robot within a Docker-based ROS 2 environment.

The authors conducted sequential experiments structured as a "capability ladder" to measure how errors from individual components compound across the entire pipeline. They evaluated 6m walking navigation accuracy, standing stability under external disturbances, and loosened fastener extraction from a real Hyundai Ioniq 5 battery pack.

The results revealed that visual-servoing grasp success dropped from 97% when tethered to 87% when free-standing, and plunged to 37% when subject to navigation-induced base pose variance. This clearly shows that ground sway and positioning errors—often overlooked in simulation—become the true bottlenecks in precision disassembly.
contributions: Demonstrated fastener removal from a real Hyundai Ioniq 5 battery pack using a full-sized humanoid (Unitree H1-2) across three levels of autonomy (tethered, free-standing, and free-standing after navigation).

Developed GOLEM, an open-source platform providing identical ROS 2/DDS interfaces across simulators (MuJoCo and IsaacLab) and the physical robot, enabling easy swapping and benchmarking of modules such as reinforcement learning and model predictive control.
Introduced an evaluation methodology termed the "Capability Ladder" to isolate error sources rung by rung, quantifying the sim-to-real gap across contact, vision, and base sway.
Presented a case study comparing multiple backends for language-conditioned spatial memory using GOLEM's shared abstract interface.

sections.heading: Why are life-sized humanoids needed for EV battery disassembly?
sections.summary: EV battery recycling disassembly is dangerous and labor-intensive, yet dedicated automation cannot adapt to diverse pack shapes. This paper introduces GOLEM, an open-source modular framework to leverage full-scale humanoids that fit directly into human work environments.
sections.details:
EV battery disassembly is an indispensable process for recovering scarce, high-value materials. However, working on packs with unknown states of charge carries severe hazards such as electric shock, smoke, toxic gases, and thermal runaway. Removing bolts alone accounts for roughly 75% of the manual labor, imposing massive physical strain on human workers.

Conventional automated equipment, such as gantry-style robotic cells, is tailored to specific packs and struggles to flexibly adapt to diverse battery geometries. Because disassembly facilities are designed around human workers, humanoid robots represent a very attractive option that can be introduced without adding ramps or specialized fixtures.

However, most recent full-body control work using reinforcement learning has focused on small platforms like the Unitree G1 (1.32m tall, 35kg). Working on a real Hyundai Ioniq 5 battery pack—measuring 1.2m by 2m and weighing 400kg—strictly requires a full-sized platform like the Unitree H1-2 (1.78m tall, 70kg, 360Nm knee torque).

To bridge this gap, this paper introduces GOLEM (Generalized Open Library of Embodied Modules), an end-to-end system architecture for the H1-2. Instead of relying on a black-box monolithic policy, GOLEM decouples locomotion, manipulation, stabilization, and navigation into standalone modules, providing a testbed for fair comparisons across simulation and reality.

captions.F1: Unitree H1-2 working in front of a Hyundai Ioniq 5 battery pack. It illustrates the advantage of a humanoid moving flexibly in human work cells while coexisting with fixed automation hardware like RAPID.

sections.heading: Prior work in full-body control, automated disassembly, and GOLEM's role
sections.summary: The authors review prior work across robotic EV disassembly, learning-based whole-body control, and robotics middleware. GOLEM is positioned as an integration platform that binds specialized tools and learning methods under shared interfaces for fair comparison and practical task execution.
sections.details:
The authors organize prior literature into three main domains:

- Robotic EV Battery Disassembly:
Most earlier efforts focused on smaller hybrid packs or task planning. While the prior RAPID system automated unbolting on 800V-class full-sized packs, peg-hole separation—extracting loosened bolts from their bores—remains a major bottleneck. GOLEM complements fixed setups like RAPID within human-centric work cells.

- Learning-Based Whole-Body Control and Mobile Manipulation:
Advanced locomotion and full-body control methods have emerged, including human motion tracking and adversarial RL like ALMI. However, monolithic end-to-end policies make it hard to objectively pinpoint the strengths and weaknesses of individual algorithms. GOLEM allows model predictive control (MPC) and reinforcement learning (RL) policies to be swapped within the exact same framework.

- Middleware and Simulation:
Many specialized tools exist, such as ROS 2, MuJoCo, IsaacLab, OMPL for motion planning, and Nav2 for navigation. Yet integrating them into a coherent full-stack system requires immense engineering effort. GOLEM dramatically lowers this integration burden by providing abstract interfaces and Docker containers.

sections.heading: A four-layer modular architecture that unifies simulation and reality
sections.summary: GOLEM consists of four layers: containerized runtime environments, hardware interfaces, core competencies (control, navigation, perception), and high-level skills (grasping, memory). Exposing identical ROS 2 interfaces across physical hardware, MuJoCo, and IsaacLab allows seamless transition from simulation to reality without code changes.
sections.details:
The overall architecture of GOLEM is organized into the four layers shown in Figure F2:

- Containerized Robot Deployment (III-A):
The system is implemented as a suite of Docker containers communicating over CycloneDDS. Simulators (MuJoCo and IsaacLab) publish the exact same ROS 2 topics and services as the physical robot, allowing users to switch between physical and virtual environments simply by changing the DDS domain.

- Hardware Interfaces (III-B):
For safety, all joint commands pass through a low-level safety controller. It instantly halts motion upon detecting torque exceeding 90% of rated limits or heartbeat loss, while also continuously monitoring physical emergency stop buttons via an Arduino. The wrists feature low-cost (~$460, 414g self-weight) force-controllable MAGPIE hands, with palm-embedded RealSense D405 cameras enabling high-precision visual servoing at close range (7 to 50cm).

- Core Competency Layer (III-C):
Lower-body control consumes base velocity commands $u_{\mathrm{base}}=(v_x, v_y, \omega_z)$ and allows hot-swapping between MPC-based control (MJPC), adversarial RL (ALMI), and the factory Unitree policy. Upper-body control combines Pink differential inverse kinematics (IK) with OMPL RRT-Connect, using a sphere-swept model (MorphIt) that accelerates self-collision checking 6.7×, from 38.8μs to 5.8μs. Navigation relies on FAST-LIO (LiDAR-IMU odometry) and Nav2.

- High-Level Skills (III-D):
Grasping skills support open-loop point cloud grasp generation as well as closed-loop palm camera visual servoing. Furthermore, spatiotemporal memory (via VLMaps or ReMEmbR) enables the robot to query the locations of out-of-view objects from past observations, allowing autonomous navigation and manipulation.

captions.F2: Overall GOLEM architecture. Modules are organized into layers—from the hardware layer unifying physical robots, MuJoCo, and IsaacLab, to lower/upper-body control, navigation, and perception, up to high-level skill layers like grasping and spatial memory.

sections.heading: Climbing the capability ladder: Real-world tests of navigation, balance, and bolt extraction
sections.summary: Experiments were structured as a Capability Ladder, adding one module at a time to track error propagation. Navigation stopped within an average radial error of 13.0cm; learning-based ALMI achieved a 93% recovery rate against pushes; and visual servoing achieved 97% bolt extraction while tethered and 87% while free-standing on the real pack.
sections.details:
Experiments were performed step-by-step to isolate how errors accumulate across capabilities:

- Locomotion and Navigation Accuracy (IV-A):
Using FAST-LIO and Nav2, walking to a goal 6m away was evaluated across 20 trials. The robot reached the goal in 19 out of 20 runs (95%), stopping with an average radial error of 13.0cm ($\sigma_x=6.83\text{cm}, \sigma_y=11.43\text{cm}$) around the target (Figure F3). This variance of roughly ±10–15cm sets the initial error tolerance required for downstream manipulation.

- Standing Disturbance Rejection (IV-B):
Pushes were applied to the pelvis using a force-sensing rod (Figure F4). Under perturbations, sampling-based MPC (MJPC) suffered monotonic degradation in center-of-mass (CoM) margin, requiring an emergency stop after an average of 4.68 seconds. In contrast, RL-based ALMI recovered and maintained positive CoM margin in 14 of 15 trials (93%). ALMI was therefore selected for all subsequent standing manipulation tasks.

- Manipulation and Fastener Extraction (IV-C):
The authors evaluated loosened bolt extraction from the real Ioniq 5 battery pack (Figure F5):
1. Tethered Support: With base sway eliminated, closed-loop visual servoing (C-VS) using the palm camera achieved a 96.7% success rate. In contrast, open-loop methods relying on a single snapshot failed entirely due to calibration errors and real-world depth noise.
2. Autonomous Standing: Standing under ALMI introduced base sway inherent to physical hardware (4.6mm RMS sway and 18.0mm maximum displacement on hardware vs 0.1mm in simulation), causing success to drop to 86.7%. Failures were caused by off-axis jamming during pull-out.
3. Standing After Navigation (Var. Stand): Factoring in base pose variance after walking, success dropped to 37%. Stopping too close to or too far from the workbench pushed the arm beyond its reachable workspace.

- Comparative Evaluation of Spatial Memory (IV-D):
In a kitchen environment (RoboCasa), spatial memory backends like VLMaps and SigLIP+FAISS were compared. Adding VLM reranking improved disambiguation of moved objects, but increased query latency by roughly 1,000×, clearly illustrating trade-offs made visible through GOLEM's shared interface.

captions.F4: Disturbance rejection comparison during standing (MJPC vs. ALMI). Black lines show applied force; green lines represent the Center of Mass (CoM) margin relative to the support polygon. ALMI (right) autonomously steps to recover even when strong pushes temporarily drive the margin negative.
captions.F5: Success rates and CoM margins for refrigerator door opening (simulation) and Ioniq 5 bolt extraction (simulation and real hardware). In real-world bolt extraction, closed-loop visual servoing (C-VS) maintains high success even while free-standing.

sections.heading: Uncovering the sim-to-real gap and looking ahead
sections.summary: GOLEM's modular design revealed that the primary failure mode in real-world tasks stems not from grasping manipulation itself, but from base positioning errors after walking. Because simulation tends to underestimate contact friction and micro-sway, module-level credit assignment and safety guarantees will be essential moving forward.
sections.details:
This paper presented GOLEM, a modular full-body autonomy framework aimed at the critical real-world application of EV battery disassembly, and validated it on a physical Unitree H1-2.

Evaluating capabilities rung by rung yielded a vital insight: the dominant cause of bolt extraction failure was not the end-effector grasping algorithm, but base placement variance (navigation error) when reaching the workstation. In future humanoid research, fine repositioning (relocalization and micro-stepping) near target objects will be decisive.

Furthermore, the experiments exposed clear limitations in digital twins. While a simulated robot appears perfectly steady, the real humanoid constantly experiences millimeters of foot sway. When combined with sensor calibration offsets and contact friction, this micro-sway completely breaks open-loop control.

When deploying humanoids into industrial environments alongside people, explainability—knowing exactly which module caused a failure—transcends academic interest to become a mandatory safety requirement. GOLEM provides a solid foundation toward that goal.

takeaways: Humanoid task failures start from the feet, not the hands: The decisive factor in bolt extraction was reaching workspace limits caused by base stopping errors (13cm on average) after navigation.

Never overtrust contact and sway in simulation: Standing sway was nearly zero (0.1mm) in simulation but reached 4.6mm RMS on physical hardware, causing open-loop grasping to fail completely. Closed-loop visual servoing via palm cameras is essential.

Right tool for the right job: RL vs. MPC: The study demonstrated a hybrid balance—adversarial RL (ALMI) excels at dynamic push recovery, whereas optimization-based IK/OMPL is superior for trajectory following and collision avoidance.
The power of modularity and shared interfaces: Providing identical ROS 2 interfaces across simulators and physical hardware dramatically simplifies algorithm swapping and fair benchmark comparisons.
limitations: A fine repositioning module after walking navigation is not yet implemented, leaving the robot unable to self-correct stopping pose errors using micro-steps before manipulation.

Precise impedance/force control for pulling bolts strictly along their vertical axis remains insufficient; when trajectory planning becomes nonlinear near joint limits, the bolt jams against the hole sidewalls and slips out of the gripper.
The IsaacLab integration currently covers only hardware interface validation and has not yet achieved full module integration on par with the MuJoCo environment.
